title: Constants, Mutability, and Immutability
learningObjectives: Explain mutability as whether a value or structure can be changed after creation.
Distinguish rebinding a variable from modifying the data it refers to.
Describe constants as names whose reassignment is restricted under a language's rules.
Explain why immutable data can make program behavior easier to reason about.
Recognize that a constant reference may still point to mutable contents in some languages.

understand.concept: Mutability describes whether stored data can be changed. Immutability means a value or structure cannot be modified after it is created, or that changes are expressed by creating a new value. A constant declaration typically restricts rebinding or reassignment of a name, but in some languages it does not make every nested object immutable.
understand.whyItMatters: Controlling changes can reduce accidental side effects, make shared data safer to reason about, and clarify which parts of a program are allowed to update state. Understanding the difference between a constant binding and immutable data prevents misleading assumptions.
understand.analogy: A permanent label on a box means you cannot rename the label's binding, but the contents of the box may still be rearranged. A truly sealed box is closer to immutable data.
understand.analogyLimit: The meaning of const, final, readonly, or immutable differs by language and may apply to a binding, a field, shallow contents, or an entire value. Check the specific language rules.

explain.narrative: A variable can be reassigned to a different value, while a mutable structure can be modified through its contents. These are separate operations. Some declarations restrict reassignment but allow mutation of an object. Immutable data structures instead avoid in-place changes, often returning a new structure for an update. Use constants for stable values and prefer immutability when it improves clarity, safety, or predictable state; do not assume every language's constant keyword deeply freezes data.

commonMistakes: Assuming a constant declaration makes an entire object deeply immutable.
Confusing changing a property's value with assigning a new value to the variable.
Using mutable shared data without considering side effects.
Assuming immutable data means a program can never change state—it may create new values.
Choosing mutability without considering intended lifetime and update behavior.
